Meta.title: carps: A Framework for Comparing N Hyperparameter Optimizers on M Benchmarks

research_question_1.value: How can we design a unified, lightweight benchmarking framework that eases the prototyping and evaluation of Hyperparameter Optimization (HPO) methods across diverse task types?
research_question_1.reason: In Section 1 (Introduction) and Section 4, the authors motivate the need for a comprehensive experimentation pipeline and a lightweight interface to glue optimizers and benchmarks together, addressing the challenge of setting up new benchmarking setups from scratch and ensuring reproducibility.

research_question_2.value: How can we select a diverse and representative subset of HPO benchmark tasks to reduce computational overhead and prevent evaluation bias from overrepresented task types?
research_question_2.reason: In Section 1 and Section 7, the authors discuss the computational infeasibility and potential bias of using all 3336 available tasks, motivating a principled way to subselect benchmark tasks with respect to diversity in the performance space.

hypothesis_1.value: The authors hypothesise that minimizing the L_infinity star discrepancy of a subset of tasks in the performance space spanned by a set of diverse optimizers will yield a representative and diverse benchmark subset.
hypothesis_1.reason: In Section 7.1, the authors propose using the L_infinity star discrepancy on the performance data of N optimizers to select k points that best cover the space, expecting it to characterize the quality of the selected sets and provide a representative subset.

hypothesis_2.value: The authors hypothesise that the rankings of HPO optimizers evaluated on the proposed subselected task sets will remain consistent across disjoint development and test subsets.
hypothesis_2.reason: In Section 7 and Appendix H.2, the authors propose using two disjoint sets (dev and test) for unbiased performance reporting and explicitly validate that the ranking remains consistent across these subsets to ensure the subsets are reliable.

experiment_1.experiment_description: Subselecting representative sets of tasks for blackbox, multi-fidelity, multi-objective, and multi-fidelity-multi-objective task types by optimizing the star discrepancy for different subset sizes k.
experiment_1.strategy: Iterative heuristic optimization of the L_infinity star discrepancy for subset sizes k in {10, 20, 30, ..., 100}. The process is performed twice to obtain disjoint dev and test sets.

experiment_2.experiment_description: Benchmarking one representative optimization method from each optimizer family on the subselected task sets for each task type to establish baselines and validate ranking consistency.
experiment_2.strategy: 20 random seeds per optimizer per task. Budget depends on dimensionality (n_trials = ceil(20 + 40*sqrt(d))).
data: Subselected tasks from carps framework (This work)

analysis_1.reason: Evaluating the star discrepancy for different subset sizes to determine the optimal size k that minimizes the discrepancy sum of both dev and test sets.
analysis_1.test: Comparison of discrepancy values across different k (lowest value selected).

Section 8.2.value: For each task type, many optimizers are not statistically significantly different. Their performance does differ on different tasks, indicating a possible complementarity... Sometimes, for the black-box task type, the order of ranks differs across the dev and test set. However, the distance of the ranks in those cases is lower than the critical difference, thus the absolute rank and the order thereof should be taken with a grain of salt.
Section 8.2.reason: Summarizes the statistical findings of the benchmarking experiment and validates ranking consistency.
data: Subselected tasks from carps framework (This work)

interpretation_1.value: The authors interpret that the subselected tasks follow the source distribution well, and the chosen subset sizes (e.g., k=30 for blackbox) effectively minimize the discrepancy sum of the development and test sets, providing a representative sample of the full task space.
interpretation_1.reason: Based on Section 7.2 and Appendix H.1, the authors interpret the low discrepancy values and the visual alignment in PCA space (Figure 4) as evidence that the subsets are representative.

interpretation_2.value: The authors interpret that many optimizers are not statistically significantly different overall, but their performance varies across different tasks, indicating complementarity. Furthermore, the ranking remains consistent across the dev and test subsets, validating the reliability of the subsets.
interpretation_2.reason: In Section 8.2 and Appendix H.2, the authors note the lack of overall statistical significance but highlight task-specific strengths and confirm that the rank order distance between dev and test sets is lower than the critical difference.

conclusion_1.value: The authors conclude that carps successfully provides a lightweight benchmarking framework with representative subselected tasks that allow for efficient, unbiased evaluation and consistent ranking of HPO optimizers. They support this by showing that the subselected tasks minimize star discrepancy and maintain consistent optimizer rankings across disjoint dev and test sets.
conclusion_1.reason: In Section 10 (Conclusion) and Section 8.2, the authors summarize that the framework and its representative subsets facilitate scalable and reliable HPO development.

suggested_research_question_1.value: How can alternative diversity measures, such as symmetrized versions of the L_infinity star discrepancy, be efficiently computed and compared for benchmark subset selection?
suggested_research_question_1.reason: The authors note that the current L_infinity star discrepancy has a tendency to select more points in the upper right corner, and suggest exploring symmetrized versions once efficient subset selection methods become available.

suggested_research_question_2.value: How can active benchmarking be implemented to dynamically select tasks and build a holistic view of an algorithm's performance across different task types?
suggested_research_question_2.reason: The authors propose moving from evaluating on all available tasks to actively selecting tasks to better characterize optimizer strengths and weaknesses.

suggested_hypothesis_1.value: The authors hypothesise that combining algorithm performance data with meta-features describing the tasks will span a more comprehensive task space for benchmark subselection.
suggested_hypothesis_1.reason: The authors state they plan to contrast their current performance-based task space with one that also uses meta-features, possibly combining both to better characterize optimizers.
